questions_for_integrator: With 16 mm sensors at 10 mm spacing across ±0.03 m, do the outer sensors give a clean signal, or do they saturate and blur the centre reading?
Does the 4 cm forward offset change (5 cm to 4 cm) reduce steering oscillation, or does it make the response too sluggish on the s-bend?
At 0.7 kg and wheel track 0.14 m, does the robot reach the course in under 3 s without wheel slip on starts?
Which track loses the line first, and does max_error reach the 0.06 m limit before the first bend?

intent: Recover line tracking by widening the sensor span from 4 cm to 6 cm with seven 16 mm sensors at 10 mm spacing, so the line stays visible when the robot drifts. Pull the sensors back slightly to y = 0.04 m to reduce lag at bends. Widen the wheel track to 0.14 m for turn authority and lower the mass to 0.7 kg for faster acceleration. I expect the first track completions and fewer line-loss events, with max_error under the 0.06 m off-track limit.
learning: Iteration 0 showed that all runs went off track with progress around 0.1 to 0.15 and 1 to 2 line-loss events, so the sensor span is the first thing to fix. If line loss remains on the tightest bend, the next step is to test the forward offset or the wheel track one change at a time. If the robot holds the line but is slow, reduce mass further or raise the wheel radius. The race data from iteration 1 will confirm whether the widened span removed the line-loss failures.
rationale: Iteration 0 raced 60 trials across oval, s-bend and slalom, and none finished. Every run ended off track, with progress only 0.10 to 0.15 and max_error about 0.06, which is exactly the off-track limit (max(0.06, 0.0125 + 0.12/4) = 0.06 m). The robot is losing the line on its first bends, not running out of time. The likely cause is the baseline sensor span: five 12 mm sensors across only 4 cm see the 25 mm tape only while the line stays within about ±2 cm, so once error grows the signal drops out and line_loss_events reach 1 to 2 per run. Widening the body does not help, because body_width/4 cannot exceed the 0.06 m floor within the allowed range (0.18 m gives 0.0575 m). So the lever is sensing, not body size. This iteration changes the sensor geometry: a span of ±0.03 m (7 sensors at 10 mm spacing) with 16 mm footprints, so the outer sensors keep a reading when the line moves toward them and the tape stays covered across larger errors. I also move the sensors back to y = 0.04 m to trim lag somewhat, and widen wheel_track to 0.14 m for more turn authority on the tightest bends. Mass drops to 0.7 kg to help acceleration toward the 1.5 m/s average needed to finish in 3 s. Wheel radius and body stay at baseline so the number of changes is limited. Expected result: fewer line-loss events, lower max_error, and the first completions on the oval and s-bend tracks. This is a hypothesis to test in the next race, not a measured result.
